feedback: If marks are counted instead of spaces (giving one too many — a fencepost error), re-sweep and count the spaces between marks; each unit is a length, not a point.
If the smaller unit gives a smaller count, recount: smaller units fit more times into the same length, so the count is larger (the inverse relationship between unit size and count).
Connect back: when reading a manufactured ruler, the numeral still means 'units of space so far', exactly as on the home-made one.
Note: a paper strip has slight thickness and is a physical approximation; the scale it represents is an idealised line of equal unit-lengths.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is iterated identical units; a numeral records units of space accumulated from zero, and the smaller the unit the larger the count for the same length.
learnerActions: Make your own paper ruler by iterating a single chosen unit-length end to end and numbering the accumulated units.
Point out that each numeral names how many whole units of space lie between the start and that mark, not a label stuck on a line.
Measure a few objects with your home-made ruler, finger-sweeping the spaces between marks and counting the spaces (unit-lengths), not the marks.
Compare counts for the same object using a smaller unit versus a larger unit and describe what changes.
activities.title: Build a ruler from iterated units

feedback: For an object spanning from 3 to 12 on a broken ruler, the correct length is 9 (end numeral minus start numeral); reporting 12 signals reading the end mark directly.

If the child refuses because 'it doesn't start at 0', affirm that the object's start can line up with any whole-numbered mark, not only 0, and the length is the difference between the end and start readings.
For tool choice, reflect why a tape or metre stick suits a table or room while a short ruler flipped repeatedly accumulates error.
activities.intendedInsight: The offset-ruler item is a classic discriminator: it separates children who treat numerals as accumulated units from those who treat them as start-signals or labels.
learnerActions: Read what a broken/offset ruler reports for an object whose end sits at a numeral other than 0 (e.g. scale starts at 3) and give the length.
Match each object (pencil, table, room) to its most appropriate measuring tool and justify the pairing.
Explain for one item whether a stated reading is the mark number or the units-of-space count.
activities.title: Broken-ruler and tool-matching diagnostic items
